Succothbenoth
suk-koth-bē'noth
n. (the idol or sacred object made by the men of Babylon after their settlement in the cities of Samaria)
From Hebrew Sukkoth Benoth, literally booths of daughters — sukkah, a booth or tabernacle, with bath, a daughter. The name has been explained as the tents in which Babylonian women were prostituted in the service of their goddess, and as a Hebrew rendering of a Babylonian divine title; the older expositors generally took the first.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Succothbenoth heads the list of the gods of the resettled nations: “And the men of Babylon made Succothbenoth, and the men of Cuth made Nergal, and the men of Hamath made Ashima” (2Ki 17:30). The name is unlike the others in the list, which are ordinary divine names; this one is a Hebrew phrase — booths of daughters — and it reads as a description rather than a title. If the common explanation is right, the men of Babylon set up in Samaria the shrine-booths in which women were given to strangers as an act of worship, a practice the Greek historians describe of Babylon and which the prophets denounce wherever Israel imitated it. Whether the phrase names a structure or a goddess, the setting is fixed by the chapter: this was introduced into the land the LORD had just emptied, into “the houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made” (2Ki 17:29), and it was practised alongside a professed fear of the LORD (2Ki 17:33). Israel had been sent into captivity for exactly this — the high places, the groves, the whoredom under every green tree — and the replacement population began doing it before the deportation ships were unloaded.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Succothbenoth; in sacred history it is the idol or sacred booth made by the men of Babylon in the cities of Samaria.

expand to see more

SUCCOTHBENOTH, n. The booths of daughters; an object of worship set up in Samaria.

It was made by the men of Babylon, whom the king of Assyria planted in the land.

The name is understood by many of the tents wherein women were prostituted to the idol.

Others take it for a Hebrew form of a Babylonian divine title.

It stands first in the list of the gods which the transplanted nations made for themselves.

Key Scripture

2Ki 17:30 — "And the men of Babylon made Succothbenoth, and the men of Cuth made Nergal, and the men of Hamath made Ashima,"

2Ki 17:29 — "Howbeit every nation made gods of their own, and put them in the houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made, every nation in their cities wherein they dwelt."

2Ki 17:24 — "And the king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Ava, and from Hamath, and from Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel: and they possessed Samaria, and dwelt in the cities thereof."

2Ki 17:33 — "They feared the LORD, and served their own gods, after the manner of the nations whom they carried away from thence."

Modern Corruption

Ritual prostitution is treated as an exotic feature of ancient religion with no modern counterpart. Scripture treats sexual sin and idolatry as one subject throughout, and the pairing is exactly as live now as it was in Samaria.

expand to see more

It is usual to read the sacred prostitution of the ancient world as a curiosity — a religious form so alien that it tells us nothing about ourselves. Scripture makes no such separation. The prophets use the same vocabulary for both sins because they are the same sin looked at from two sides: Israel goes a whoring after other gods, and Israel goes a whoring in the ordinary sense, and Hosea was told to marry a wife of whoredoms to make the point unmissable. Where a false god is worshipped, the body follows; where the body is given away, a god is being served.

Paul reasons in precisely this way to a Gentile church in a city famous for its temple women. He rehearses Israel's wilderness sins — “Neither be ye idolaters, as were some of them” (1Co 10:7), “Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed” (1Co 10:8) — as one connected warning, and he names covetousness itself as idolatry (Col 3:5). The booths of daughters have not disappeared from the world; they have been rebuilt as an industry, and the worship they serve is the same. The answer Paul gives is not a strategy but a fact of ownership: “For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God&#39;s” (1Co 6:20).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Sukkoth Benoth (H5524), booths of daughters; sukkah (H5521), booth, tabernacle; bath (H1323), daughter; zanah (H2181), to go a whoring, commit fornication; bamah (H1116), high place.

expand to see more

Hebrew Sukkoth Benoth (H5524) — Succothbenoth; the booths of daughters.

Hebrew sukkah (H5521) — a booth; the same word as the feast of tabernacles.

Hebrew bath (H1323) — daughter; the second element of the name.

Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to go a whoring; used of both idolatry and fornication.

Hebrew bamah (H1116) — high place; where these things were set up.

Usage

"“The men of Babylon made Succothbenoth” — an imported worship in an emptied land."

"“The houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made” — old shrines put to new use."

"“They feared the LORD, and served their own gods” — the settlement's permanent arrangement."
